The Lottery and the Preface do worse damage than strain: they falsify Belief Consistency and Belief Closure, the most natural rational norms for binary belief, while credence norms handle both cases comfortably. Numbers buy the sizes of the gaps between confidences at a price, since precise credences over-attribute exactness and force every pair of propositions into a single ranking. Beliefs and credences may both be real without any general systematic bridge between them, the way a topographic map and a satellite image record the same square mile without either being derivable from the other.
signature_moves: Runs the physicist example: she believes fusion is viable and believes her brakes will stop the car, yet stakes her life on one belief every morning, and he asks his opponent to name the difference in purely binary terms.
Invents the Simple Binarist, a character who ascribes only belief, disbelief, and suspension, then piles up doxastic phenomena that character cannot describe.
Presses the Lottery and the Preface as counterexamples rather than puzzles, arguing they show Belief Consistency and Belief Closure to be false rather than merely demanding.

Separates theoretical from practical rationality using Pascal's Wager: even if believing in God pays, an agent whose evidence points to atheism makes a rational mistake in believing, so evidence-responsiveness answers to its own standard.

Walks down the confidence scale to test the Lockean threshold, rejecting certainty as the cutoff because we rationally believe things we are not certain of, and finding nothing that fixes the line between 50% and 100%.
Concedes the costs of his own view: assigning precise credences attributes gap sizes that may not exist and destroys the incommensurability between, say, election questions and climate questions.
key_works: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences (2022), ch. 1, 'Beliefs and Degrees of Belief'
Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 2: Arguments, Challenges, Alternatives (2022)
Quitting Certainties: A Bayesian Framework Modeling Degrees of Belief (2013)

signature_attack.name: The Brake Pedal Test
signature_attack.description: He names two things you say you believe, asks which one you would bet your life on this afternoon, and makes you explain that difference using only the words believe, disbelieve, and suspend.

philosophers.thinking_text: Titelbaum checks how confident he actually is...
philosophers.defeat_text: Fair enough, you have held the line. I only ever claimed that degrees of belief add something, and you have shown me that belief talk still earns its keep. Keep the brake pedal case in mind anyway.
philosophers.victory_text: Read the Lottery again before you argue with me next time. If you really believe of each ticket that it loses, you believe no ticket wins, and then why did you buy one?

philosophers.name: Susan Wolf
philosophers.core_assumptions: A moral saint is a person whose every action is as morally good as possible, and Wolf denies that such a life makes a good personal ideal for anyone to hold. The moral virtues, present all at once in one person and to an extreme degree, crowd out nonmoral virtues that are genuinely worth having: gourmet cooking, a sarcastic wit, Victorian novels, a decent backhand. Utilitarian and Kantian saints escape none of this, because each must value his fishing trip or his cello playing under a further description, either 'a contribution to the general happiness' or 'a manifestation of respect for the moral law', which gives him one thought too many. Wolf therefore argues that morality should not serve as a comprehensive guide to conduct, and she sets beside the moral point of view a second one, the point of view of individual perfection, from which we ask what kinds of persons it would be good to be. Her target is not the content of any moral theory but the metamoral assumption that it is always better to be morally better.
signature_moves: Splits sainthood into the Loving Saint, whose happiness lies in the happiness of others, and the Rational Saint, who feels the sacrifice as sacrifice, then convicts the first of blindness to what the world offers and the second of self-hatred or a fear of damnation.
Itemizes the nonmoral goods sainthood forecloses, from the Marx Brothers to haute cuisine to high fashion, until the perfected life starts to look strangely barren.
Presses Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' charge against utilitarian and Kantian saints alike: they value literature or roses only under a description that licenses the activity morally.
Grants the opponent's theory intact and attacks the assumption standing behind it, so that neither utilitarianism nor Kantianism is refuted from the inside.
Tests a proposed ideal by asking whether you would want the people you love, or your own children, to achieve it.

Separates the moral point of view from the point of view of individual perfection and denies that the second collapses into self-interest, since it asks what interests it would be good for a person to have.
key_works: Meaning in Life and Why It Matters

signature_attack.name: One Thought Too Many
signature_attack.description: She grants your principle, then asks what you must say to yourself before you may enjoy a friend, a novel, or a good meal, and whether a person should have to think that thought at all.

philosophers.thinking_text: Wolf wonders whether she would want her children to turn out this way...
philosophers.defeat_text: You have made your ideal look attractive as well as consistent, which is the harder half of the job and more than I managed for the saint. Keep the argument. Keep the Marx Brothers too.
philosophers.victory_text: You attacked a saint I never defended. Read the middle of the paper again, where the utilitarian and the Kantian each get a turn, and notice that I let both theories stand.

opening_statements.text: Picture the person this course is training you to become. Every action as morally good as possible. Patient, considerate, charitable in thought as well as in deed, and very, very nice. He may enjoy an episode of Father Knows Best; he cannot in good conscience laugh at a Marx Brothers movie, since sarcastic wit requires a certain pleasure in other people's flaws. He will never cook a pate de canard en croute. Aristotle promised you a full and flourishing character. I say the moral virtues, all of them at once and to the limit, crowd the interesting ones out.

move_hints.counterexample: Name a real person whose moral seriousness produced wit or art rather than crowding it out, such as Chesterton's Father Brown, whom Wolf herself concedes we prefer to St. Francis.
move_hints.reductio: Push her list further: if every hour spent on the oboe is an hour not spent on Oxfam, her own philosophy seminar goes on the chopping block along with the pate.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: Ask whether the goods she is defending, gourmet cooking and high fashion among them, are excellences or merely expensive tastes she happens to enjoy.
move_hints.framework_shift: Argue as Aristotle would that her nonmoral virtues are already parts of a well-ordered character, so the saint she describes is not the virtuous person but a distortion of one.

opening_statements.text: Suppose you are a good utilitarian, or a good Kantian, and you take an evening off to read Tolstoy. Why is that allowed? The utilitarian answers that his enjoyment forms part of the general happiness, and he stands ready to give up the book the moment the calculation turns. The Kantian answers that cultivating his powers manifests reverence for the moral law. Bernard Williams called this one thought too many. I call it a shallow way to love a novel. Show me how your theory lets a person simply love the thing in front of them.

move_hints.counterexample: Describe a utilitarian who loves Tolstoy directly and never runs the calculation, and ask whether Wolf can show that such a person has abandoned utilitarianism rather than internalized it.
move_hints.reductio: If valuing something under a further description makes the attachment shallow, then Wolf's own perfectionist reasons for loving the novel are one thought too many as well.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: Ask what she thinks a person should say when the evening with Tolstoy really does come at the cost of a life that could have been saved.
move_hints.framework_shift: Take Singer's line: the extra thought is the point, and a world where people run the calculation feeds more children than a world where they simply love their novels.

opening_statements.text: Grant everything I have said and neither Mill nor Kant is refuted. Their theories survive intact. What breaks is the quieter assumption standing behind them, that it is always better to be morally better. Mother Theresa is a morally better person than Katharine Hepburn, and I will not pretend otherwise. I still say a young person may reasonably take Hepburn as her model. A person may be perfectly wonderful without being perfectly moral. Defend the assumption if you can: tell me why the moral point of view gets to rank every life, including the ones lived well outside it.

move_hints.counterexample: Point to a case where we plainly do think more moral is better, such as a bystander who saves a drowning child at real cost, and press her to say where the ranking stops.
move_hints.reductio: If moral judgments do not outrank perfectionist ones, then a person could rationally choose style over rescue, and Wolf has licensed exactly the excuse she says our reasons are not.
move_hints.socratic_questioning: Ask what makes the point of view of individual perfection objective rather than a dressed-up report of what Wolf and her friends happen to admire.
move_hints.framework_shift: Use Kant against her: duties of benevolence and self-perfection come from reason itself, so a second point of view outside morality has no authority to override them.

philosophers.name: Iris Marion Young
philosophers.core_assumptions: Young treats oppression as a condition of groups produced by ordinary institutions rather than by a tyrant's decree, with its causes lodged in unquestioned norms, habits, symbols, and the collective consequences of people following the rules of their jobs. She holds that justice reaches past distribution to decisionmaking procedures, the division of labor, and culture, so a theory that asks only who gets how much cannot say what is wrong with marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, or systematic violence. Social groups constitute individuals rather than being assembled out of them: group affinity has the character Heidegger called thrownness, something a person finds herself already inside and then takes up in some way. Because different combinations of factors constitute the oppression of different groups, Young refuses one essential definition and offers five criteria instead, any one of which suffices for calling a group oppressed. She claims these criteria are objective and can adjudicate disputes about whether a group is oppressed, while conceding that they function as criteria and not as a full theory of oppression.
signature_moves: Separates structural oppression from tyranny by pointing at the everyday practices of a well-intentioned liberal society, where the conscious actions of many individuals reproduce oppression while those people are usually simply doing their jobs or living their lives.

Pays out the distributive remedy first and then asks what is left over: give a marginalized old person a comfortable material life inside decent institutions, and uselessness, boredom, and lack of self-respect remain.

Sorts a group's situation by which faces apply, so that working-class people count as exploited and powerless while, if employed and white, they escape marginalization and violence, and gay men suffer cultural imperialism and violence without being exploited qua gay.

Answers the individualist by distinguishing a social group from both an aggregate and an association: George Sher's arbitrary classifications and any voluntary club alike put the individual ahead of the collective, whereas group meanings partly constitute who people already are.

Turns the invisibility of dominant norms back on the dominant group, since cultural imperialism installs one group's experience as the unremarkable universal and leaves white males, escaping group marking, free to appear as individuals.

Brings violence inside a theory of justice by relocating its wrongness from the individual attacker to the social practice around him, and to the daily knowledge of liability that every member of a targeted group carries.
key_works: Justice and the Politics of Difference
Throwing Like a Girl and Other Essays

signature_attack.name: No Tyrant Required
signature_attack.description: She hands you a harm nobody intended, produced by rules that everyone involved is dutifully following, and asks your account of justice to say what is wrong with it.

philosophers.thinking_text: Young looks past the tyrant to the rules everyone is following...
philosophers.defeat_text: You located the injustice without needing a villain to pin it on, and you kept the group in view while you did it. Take the five faces with you. They are criteria for judging, and I never claimed they were the whole theory.
philosophers.victory_text: You answered a question about groups by telling me about individuals. Go back to the chapter, read what separates a social group from an aggregate, and then tell me again that we should all just be treated as persons.
